title: Ajiaco Bogotano
subtitle: Bogota potato and chicken soup with guasca herb
excerpt: A thick, hearty potato and chicken soup from the Colombian highlands, flavoured with guasca herb and served with cream and capers. This recipe serves 6 and takes about 1 hour 20 minutes. It is the soup of Bogota, eaten on cold weekday lunches and rainy Sunday afternoons alike.
sourceNotes: Ajiaco is the emblematic soup of Bogota and the surrounding Cundinamarca region. Its use of three types of potato reflects the extraordinary potato biodiversity of the Andes. The dish was eaten before Spanish colonisation and has remained a cornerstone of highland Colombian cooking for centuries.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The soup base can be made a day ahead without the cream or capers. Reheat and add the garnishes when serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: A dried herb native to the Colombian Andes with a mild, slightly cheesy and artichoke-like flavour. It is the ingredient that gives ajiaco its distinctive taste and cannot be substituted. Available dried in Latin American food shops.

content.text: This recipe serves 6 and takes about 1 hour 20 minutes. The soup uses three different types of potato on purpose: one breaks down completely to thicken the broth, one holds its shape and one sits somewhere in between. This combination of textures is what makes ajiaco different from a regular chicken and potato soup.

Without it the soup is still good, but it is not ajiaco. Order it in advance if you need to. The corn goes in on the bone, cut into rounds, and is eaten alongside the soup.

Place the chicken thighs in a large pot with the onion halves, garlic cloves and the bunch of coriander. Cover with 2 litres of cold water and bring to the boil. Skim any foam from the surface, then reduce to a steady simmer and cook for 25 minutes.
Remove the chicken and set aside to cool. Remove and discard the onion and coriander bunch. Leave the stock in the pot.

Peel and chop all three types of potato: 500g papa criolla or waxy yellow potato (cut into small chunks), 400g floury potato like Maris Piper (cut into chunks), and 300g new potatoes (left whole or halved). Add all the potato to the stock along with 2 ears of corn cut into rounds.

Add 2 tbsp dried guasca herb to the pot. Bring back to a simmer and cook for 25 to 30 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the floury potato has broken down and thickened the broth and the waxy potato is tender.
Shred the cooled chicken, discarding the skin and bones, and stir back into the pot. Season well with salt. Simmer for 5 more minutes to heat the chicken through.
Ladle into deep bowls. Serve with sour cream, capers, fresh coriander and lime wedges on the side for people to add as they like.

attrs.cause: The floury potato did not break down sufficiently to thicken the soup
attrs.fix: Mash a few large spoonfuls of potato against the side of the pot and stir them into the broth. Alternatively, remove a ladleful of soup, blend it, and stir it back in.

attrs.symptom: Soup tastes flat without the guasca
attrs.cause: Guasca is unavailable and no substitute provides the same flavour
attrs.fix: Without guasca, boost the flavour with extra coriander stalks added while simmering and removed before serving. A teaspoon of dried epazote (a Mexican herb, more widely available) adds a different but not unpleasant herbal note.

attrs.symptom: Corn is tough and difficult to eat
attrs.cause: Corn needs a long simmer to become tender in soup
attrs.fix: Make sure the corn simmers for the full 25 to 30 minutes in the broth. If the kernels are still firm, continue simmering for another 10 to 15 minutes.

content.text: Bogota sits high in the Andes at 2,600 metres, where it is often cold and overcast. Ajiaco is the answer to that climate: a soup thick enough to be a meal, eaten at lunchtime in restaurants and homes throughout the city. It is also the soup served at special occasions across Colombia, brought out for family gatherings and celebrations. The three-potato combination is non-negotiable to anyone from Bogota.
